exam_title: Fortinet Enterprise Networking & Security — Daily Technical Assessment

questions.stem: Which TLS 1.3 hybrid group is explicitly listed for proxy-mode deep inspection?

choices.text: X25519MLKEM768, combining X25519 and ML-KEM-768
choices.feedback: The documented hybrid group combines a classical X25519 component with ML-KEM-768.

choices.text: P-256 ECDSA with RSA-2048 certificate signatures
choices.feedback: The choice describes certificate signature algorithms, not a TLS key-exchange group.

choices.text: AES-256-GCM with a conventional RSA key exchange
choices.feedback: Cipher selection does not identify the negotiated key-exchange group.

choices.text: X25519 alone without any post-quantum component
choices.feedback: This omits the ML-KEM component required for the hybrid exchange.

questions.stem: A capture shows X25519MLKEM768 in the browser ClientHello. What does it prove?

choices.text: The upstream origin negotiated that group with FortiGate
choices.feedback: The upstream negotiation is a separate TLS session in proxy inspection.

choices.text: The client offered a supported hybrid key-exchange group
choices.feedback: ClientHello proves the client offer on that leg; capture the upstream leg to prove its negotiation.

choices.text: The firewall inspected every application protocol in the flow
choices.feedback: A key-share offer says nothing about protocol coverage or inspection policy selection.

choices.text: The server certificate chain passed the proxy trust check
choices.feedback: The ClientHello does not validate the origin certificate or client trust.

questions.stem: Which TLS consumer is explicitly outside the documented hybrid ML-KEM support?

choices.text: HTTPS, including the documented HTTP versions
choices.feedback: HTTPS is included in the documented protocol support.

choices.text: DNS over TLS through proxy deep inspection
choices.feedback: DNS over TLS is included in the documented proxy-mode support.

choices.text: SIP over TLS and FortiGuard URL-filter TLS
choices.feedback: Fortinet explicitly lists SIP over TLS and URL-filter TLS to FortiGuard as unsupported for hybrid ML-KEM.

choices.text: POP3, IMAPS and SMTPS with deep inspection
choices.feedback: The listed mail protocols are included in the supported set.

questions.stem: Which policy setting is essential in the documented deep-inspection example?

choices.text: Use flow mode and leave the SSL profile unattached
choices.feedback: Flow mode does not meet the documented proxy-mode feature requirement.

choices.text: Enable certificate inspection without proxy termination on this policy
choices.feedback: Certificate inspection alone does not provide the documented deep-inspection path.

choices.text: Apply the profile only to a local-in management policy
choices.feedback: A local-in policy handles traffic to the FortiGate, not transit client sessions.

choices.text: Attach the profile to a policy using proxy inspection
choices.feedback: The example attaches the cloned deep-inspection profile to a firewall policy with proxy inspection.

questions.stem: In the blueprint workflow, what does the certificate template represent?

choices.text: Reusable certificate-generation parameters referenced by a blueprint
choices.feedback: The template defines certificate parameters; the blueprint references it during model-device creation.

choices.text: A live certificate already installed on a managed FortiGate
choices.feedback: A live certificate is an output artifact, not the reusable template.

choices.text: A policy package containing firewall rules and address objects
choices.feedback: A policy package is a separate configuration object.

choices.text: A model device record that waits for discovery authorization
choices.feedback: A model device is the offline device representation, not the certificate template.

questions.stem: At which lifecycle point does FortiManager generate the model-device certificate?

choices.text: When the administrator first opens the certificate template editor
choices.feedback: Opening the editor does not instantiate a model device.

choices.text: When the model device or model HA cluster is added
choices.feedback: The documented flow generates the certificate when the model device or HA model is added.

choices.text: Only after the physical FortiGate completes its first firmware upgrade
choices.feedback: Firmware upgrade is not the certificate-generation trigger.

choices.text: When the blueprint is renamed after discovery finishes
choices.feedback: Renaming a blueprint does not retroactively create the model certificate.

questions.stem: An administrator edits a blueprint already used by ten model devices. What changes?

choices.text: All existing model devices are rewritten right away
choices.feedback: Existing models are not automatically rewritten by blueprint edits.

choices.text: Only previously discovered devices inherit the new settings
choices.feedback: Discovery does not convert a blueprint edit into a retroactive update.

choices.text: Only later-added devices inherit the edited blueprint settings
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents that blueprint edits affect devices added after the edit, not existing models.

choices.text: Changes apply after each device is re-authorized in Fabric
choices.feedback: Fabric re-authorization is unrelated to blueprint revision scope.

questions.stem: Which check best proves certificate-template processing for a new model device?

choices.text: Confirm the blueprint name appears in the ADOM inventory
choices.feedback: The ADOM list proves object placement, not certificate generation.

choices.text: Check that the model device shows a green discovery icon
choices.feedback: A discovery icon proves connectivity/authorization, not certificate creation.

choices.text: Verify the policy package includes its expected default route
choices.feedback: A default route in a policy package is unrelated to certificate-template processing.

choices.text: Inspect the generated certificate in system:certificates after creation
choices.feedback: The generated certificate is visible in system:certificates after the model device is added.

questions.stem: Why can logs remain in FortiView after a device is deleted?

choices.text: SQL analytics rows remain after raw and archive files are removed
choices.feedback: FortiAnalyzer removes raw/archive material but leaves already-inserted SQL analytics rows until cleanup.

choices.text: The log collector can recreate the deleted device automatically
choices.feedback: A remaining SQL row does not mean the collector recreated the device.

choices.text: Device deletion always preserves the original raw archive packets
choices.feedback: The documented behavior removes raw files and archive packets.

choices.text: FortiView reads only from the live Device Manager inventory
choices.feedback: FortiView can query analytics rows even when the device is absent from inventory.

questions.stem: One deleted device leaves stale analytics rows in a known ADOM. What is the narrowest documented rebuild?

choices.text: Rebuild the entire appliance SQL database immediately
choices.feedback: A full rebuild is broader than necessary when the ADOM is known.

choices.text: Rebuild the SQL database for that device's ADOM
choices.feedback: The Administration Guide permits rebuilding the SQL database for the affected ADOM.

choices.text: Delete the ADOM and recreate all managed devices
choices.feedback: Deleting the ADOM destroys far more configuration and is not the documented cleanup.

choices.text: Disable Analytics logging globally for every ADOM
choices.feedback: Disabling all Analytics logging does not remove existing rows.

questions.stem: What is special about global Automatically Delete settings?

choices.text: Apply only to raw log files for one deleted device
choices.feedback: The setting is global, not limited to one device's raw logs.

choices.text: Change archive retention but never analytics retention across ADOMs
choices.feedback: The guide describes their effect on deleted-device logs and broader storage cleanup.

choices.text: They override other log-storage settings at the global level
choices.feedback: Fortinet states that global automatic deletion settings override other log-storage settings and apply to all ADOMs.

choices.text: Remove inventory entries without touching stored log data
choices.feedback: The control concerns log files, not just Device Manager inventory.

questions.stem: A device is absent from Device Manager but old rows still query. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: The device is still sending new logs over an active tunnel
choices.feedback: Residual historical rows do not prove new ingestion is occurring.

choices.text: Raw archive deletion must have failed during device removal
choices.feedback: Raw/archive deletion can succeed while SQL rows remain.

choices.text: The SQL database is necessarily corrupt and unusable now
choices.feedback: Residual rows are expected behavior and do not establish database corruption.

choices.text: Device deletion completed while SQL analytics history remains visible
choices.feedback: This is the documented separation between inventory/raw deletion and SQL analytics cleanup.

questions.stem: What does the relay agent place in GIADDR for a client DHCP request?

choices.text: The relay interface address identifying the client subnet
choices.feedback: GIADDR identifies the relay/client subnet so the DHCP server can choose the correct scope.

choices.text: The DHCP server address selected as the preferred target
choices.feedback: The target server is configured separately from GIADDR.

choices.text: The client's MAC address encoded as a four-byte address
choices.feedback: A MAC address is not the GIADDR field.

choices.text: The Option 82 circuit identifier from the access port
choices.feedback: Circuit identity is carried in Option 82, not GIADDR.

questions.stem: How does FortiSwitch handle multiple configured DHCP relay targets?

choices.text: It sends to the first target and waits before trying the next
choices.feedback: The documented behavior is fan-out, not sequential failover.

choices.text: It forwards a copy of the client request to each target
choices.feedback: FortiSwitch supports up to eight relay targets and forwards copies of the message to them.

choices.text: It hashes the client MAC to choose one server permanently
choices.feedback: No MAC-hash server-selection behavior is documented for this relay.

choices.text: It merges all server scopes into one virtual address pool
choices.feedback: DHCP servers keep their own scopes; the relay does not merge them.

questions.stem: Which configuration combination is prohibited on the same interface?

choices.text: Enabling DHCP snooping while using a DHCP server
choices.feedback: The guide distinguishes DHCP snooping and permits it with a DHCP server.

choices.text: Configuring two DHCP relay target addresses
choices.feedback: Multiple relay targets are supported, up to eight.

choices.text: Enabling both the DHCP server and DHCP relay
choices.feedback: FortiSwitch documentation says DHCP server and DHCP relay cannot be enabled simultaneously on one interface.

choices.text: Using Option 82 insertion with a DHCP relay
choices.feedback: Option 82 is an optional relay behavior.

questions.stem: A DISCOVER leaves the switch but no OFFER reaches the client. What should be checked next?

choices.text: The client's wireless multicast group membership table
choices.feedback: Wireless IGMP membership is unrelated to DHCP relay.

choices.text: Whether the FortiSwitch policy package contains a certificate
choices.feedback: Certificate templates do not control DHCP scope selection.

choices.text: The FortiManager blueprint revision used for the switch
choices.feedback: A blueprint revision does not prove the DHCP server return path.

choices.text: Server scope selection and the route back to GIADDR
choices.feedback: The DHCP server must select the right scope and route its offer back to the relay GIADDR.

questions.stem: What is the primary job of IGMP snooping in the FortiAP multicast design?

choices.text: Track listeners and prune APs without group members
choices.feedback: IGMP snooping tracks group membership so the controller can avoid sending to APs with no listener.

choices.text: Convert every multicast packet into per-client unicast frames
choices.feedback: Multicast enhancement performs the multicast-to-unicast transformation.

choices.text: Disable multicast traffic when the SSID reaches its threshold
choices.feedback: The threshold controls enhancement, not all multicast traffic.

choices.text: Select the best RF channel based on multicast bitrate
choices.feedback: RF channel selection is a separate radio-management function.

questions.stem: What does multicast-enhance change on an AP with interested clients?

choices.text: Convert unicast TCP sessions into one shared multicast stream
choices.feedback: The feature does not convert TCP unicast into multicast.

choices.text: Convert multicast delivery into per-client wireless unicast copies
choices.feedback: Multicast enhancement changes wireless delivery into client-specific unicast transmissions.

choices.text: Create separate IGMP groups for every associated wireless station
choices.feedback: IGMP membership is observed; the feature does not create arbitrary groups.

choices.text: Send the stream to every managed AP regardless of membership
choices.feedback: Snooping is intended to prune APs without listeners.

questions.stem: What happens when SSID client count exceeds me-disable-thresh?

choices.text: IGMP snooping is disabled and all APs receive each group
choices.feedback: IGMP snooping is a separate membership-pruning control.

choices.text: The SSID rejects all new clients until multicast stops
choices.feedback: The documented behavior does not block client associations.

choices.text: Multicast enhancement is disabled for that SSID above threshold
choices.feedback: The threshold is a client-count gate that disables multicast enhancement above the configured value.

choices.text: The controller moves the SSID to another RF band
choices.feedback: RF band selection is unrelated to the enhancement threshold.

questions.stem: Which command is useful for inspecting VAP multicast group membership?

choices.text: diagnose switch-controller switch-info 802.1X
choices.feedback: The switch-controller command is for switch authentication status.

choices.text: diagnose sys sdwan health-check
choices.feedback: The SD-WAN command inspects WAN health checks.

choices.text: diagnose vpn ike gateway list
choices.feedback: The IKE command inspects IPsec gateway state.

choices.text: diagnose wireless-controller wlac -c vap-mcgrp
choices.feedback: The documented command displays VAP multicast group information.

questions.stem: What is the core difference between Archive/Purge and database backup?

choices.text: Archive/Purge ages log records; backup protects system state
choices.feedback: Archive/Purge is a log-retention lifecycle; backup/restore protects system state.

choices.text: Archive/Purge copies the full appliance image to remote storage
choices.feedback: The guide distinguishes database archive from backup/restore.

choices.text: Backup removes aged logs after importing archive records
choices.feedback: Backup is not the archive import operation.

choices.text: Both operations delete live records on the same schedule
choices.feedback: The controls have separate schedules and effects.

questions.stem: What does importing archived FortiNAC data do?

choices.text: Replaces the live database with the archive snapshot
choices.feedback: Import archived data is not a full database restore.

choices.text: Adds archived records back without overwriting existing records
choices.feedback: FortiNAC documents import as additive; it adds archived records rather than replacing current data.

choices.text: Deletes current records before loading the archived records
choices.feedback: The documented behavior does not delete current records first.

choices.text: Replays only the archive file names without restoring records
choices.feedback: The import restores records, not just file names.

questions.stem: A Database Archive/Purge failure begins after a remote backup server key changes. What is the first check?

choices.text: Reduce the log retention age to zero and rerun the job
choices.feedback: Changing age does not repair SSH identity or transport trust.

choices.text: Delete the remote backup directory and recreate the schedule
choices.feedback: Deleting the remote directory is destructive and not the first diagnostic step.

choices.text: Test the SSH connection and verify the remote host key
choices.feedback: The historical FortiNAC scenario identifies SSH key mismatch and recommends testing the connection.

choices.text: Disable the database archive feature and purge rows manually
choices.feedback: Manual row deletion bypasses the supported archive/purge transaction.

questions.stem: Why must archive age and scheduled task cadence be reviewed together?

choices.text: The archive job runs only after a time-zone change
choices.feedback: Time-zone changes are not the archive scheduling trigger.

choices.text: A shorter age setting automatically increases remote backup capacity
choices.feedback: Retention age does not create additional remote storage capacity.

choices.text: The schedule controls remote Entra group synchronization timing
choices.feedback: Entra ID synchronization is unrelated to FortiNAC database retention.

choices.text: A long interval can delay purge beyond its intended age
choices.feedback: Age eligibility is evaluated when the scheduled task runs, so cadence affects when records are archived and purged.

questions.stem: Where do Entra ID groups appear for FortiNAC-F policy matching?

choices.text: Under Who/What > Groups when building User/Host Profiles
choices.feedback: The 7.6.5 release notes state that mapped Entra groups appear under Who/What > Groups.

choices.text: Only in the local administrator role editor
choices.feedback: Administrator roles are not the group-mapping destination.

choices.text: Only in the FortiGate firewall address object database
choices.feedback: FortiGate address objects are a different product object model.

choices.text: Inside the FortiPAM secret policy folder list
choices.feedback: FortiPAM secret folders are unrelated to NAC identity mapping.

questions.stem: How are endpoint-compliance policies evaluated when several match?

choices.text: All matching policies run their scans at the same time
choices.feedback: The documented model is ordered first-match, not parallel execution.

choices.text: The first matching policy in the ordered list is applied
choices.feedback: FortiNAC-F applies the first matching policy and its compliance configuration.

choices.text: The last policy always overrides earlier profile matches
choices.feedback: Later policies are not guaranteed to override the first match.

choices.text: Entra ID selects a policy without FortiNAC evaluation
choices.feedback: Entra supplies groups; FortiNAC evaluates its own policy list.

questions.stem: An Entra group is visible in Who/What > Groups. What does that prove?

choices.text: Every Entra user is automatically a member of that group
choices.feedback: Group visibility does not imply universal membership.

choices.text: A matching compliance policy has already executed on the endpoint
choices.feedback: A group object alone does not prove policy execution.

choices.text: The group was exposed for policy use, not user membership
choices.feedback: Group visibility proves discovery/projection; membership and policy match require separate verification.

choices.text: The MDM connector mapped device ownership into Host Role
choices.feedback: MDM ownership mapping is a different identity signal.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes Entra remote groups from MDM ownership mapping?

choices.text: Both features map only device serial numbers into host roles
choices.feedback: Neither feature is limited to serial-number host-role mapping.

choices.text: Remote groups are used only for SNMP trap enrichment
choices.feedback: SNMP trap enrichment is unrelated to Entra group matching.

choices.text: MDM ownership directly creates an Entra directory group
choices.feedback: MDM does not create directory groups in Entra ID.

choices.text: Remote groups supply directory identity; MDM supplies device metadata
choices.feedback: The selected feature maps directory groups for profile matching; MDM ownership maps endpoint metadata.

questions.stem: What is the primary distinction between cluster HA and load-balancing HA?

choices.text: Cluster syncs full configuration; load balancing syncs a subset
choices.feedback: FortiAuthenticator describes active-passive cluster synchronization versus active-active load balancing with a limited sync set.

choices.text: Both modes synchronize every service and every local setting
choices.feedback: The load-balancing mode intentionally synchronizes only selected categories.

choices.text: Load balancing is active-passive with a shared virtual IP
choices.feedback: Load balancing is active-active, not active-passive shared-IP failover.

choices.text: Cluster mode is active-active across ten remote sites
choices.feedback: Cluster mode is not the geographically distributed ten-LB design.

questions.stem: Which object set is included in documented load-balancing synchronization?

choices.text: Every FSSO setting, LDAP tree and local network interface
choices.feedback: FSSO and LDAP tree settings are not part of the documented sync set.

choices.text: Users, groups, tokens, realms and selected authentication services
choices.feedback: The documented set includes identity objects and selected SAML, RADIUS, OAuth and TACACS+ services.

choices.text: All system administration settings and every local certificate store
choices.feedback: The load-balancing sync list is narrower than all system settings.

choices.text: Only the HA heartbeat interface and management IP addresses
choices.feedback: Heartbeat and management addresses configure HA connectivity, not the object sync set.

questions.stem: A user synchronizes but the LDAP tree does not appear on an LB. What is likely?

choices.text: The user sync proves the entire database is corrupt
choices.feedback: Partial object sync is expected and does not prove database corruption.

choices.text: The load balancer must be converted to an active-passive member
choices.feedback: Changing HA mode is a design decision, not the first diagnosis.

choices.text: The LDAP tree is outside load-balancing synchronization scope
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents that LDAP tree settings do not synchronize in load-balancing mode.

choices.text: The missing tree proves the primary never accepted the user
choices.feedback: The user synchronization is evidence that at least some objects did replicate.

questions.stem: When is active-passive cluster mode the better design choice?

choices.text: Use when each remote site needs separate unsynchronized policy settings
choices.feedback: Independent site policies may favor a different design, not full config sync.

choices.text: Use when only RADIUS traffic must reach ten remote locations
choices.feedback: Load balancing is designed for distributed authentication load.

choices.text: Use when LDAP trees must remain unique on every LB node
choices.feedback: Unique LDAP trees conflict with the shared-primary sync model.

choices.text: Use when full configuration synchronization is required on every node
choices.feedback: Cluster mode synchronizes configuration and is appropriate when full config replication is required.

questions.stem: Which license model is required for wildcard remote-user support?

choices.text: The Concurrent Logon license model only
choices.feedback: FortiPAM documents wildcard users as functional only under Concurrent Logon licensing.

choices.text: Named-user licensing with static accounts per person
choices.feedback: Static named users defeat the wildcard feature's purpose.

choices.text: API-only licensing with JWT users and no groups
choices.feedback: API/JWT user types are not the wildcard remote-user type.

choices.text: A perpetual license with remote login disabled
choices.feedback: The documentation does not describe this restriction as a perpetual-license feature.

questions.stem: What takes precedence when wildcard matching and auto-provision rules both apply?

choices.text: The wildcard user always overrides each auto-provision rule
choices.feedback: This reverses the documented precedence.

choices.text: The auto-provision rule has higher priority during matching
choices.feedback: FortiPAM states that auto-provision rules take high priority when wildcard matching is enabled.

choices.text: The remote server decides based on each user's display name
choices.feedback: Display name is not the documented priority selector.

choices.text: The secret policy selects identity before user authentication
choices.feedback: Secret policy is evaluated after the user obtains a session.

questions.stem: Why should a wildcard remote user not receive an approval role?

choices.text: Wildcard users cannot authenticate with LDAP credentials
choices.feedback: Remote authentication is supported for wildcard users.

choices.text: Approval roles require a local-only FortiPAM password
choices.feedback: The restriction is not about local password storage.

choices.text: Approval roles generate notifications requiring a concrete recipient
choices.feedback: FortiPAM warns against assigning wildcard users to notification-generating features such as approval roles.

choices.text: Concurrent Logon licensing disables all secret approvals
choices.feedback: The feature does not globally disable approvals; it limits wildcard assignment.

questions.stem: Which identity selector is valid for a Remote User entry?

choices.text: Select both a remote group and server as one OR match
choices.feedback: The wizard does not define a combined OR selection.

choices.text: Select an Entra group plus a FortiGate address object together
choices.feedback: FortiGate address objects are not remote user identity sources.

choices.text: Choose a local API user and JWT user in the same record
choices.feedback: User types are separate records, not combined in one remote-user entry.

choices.text: Choose either one remote group or one remote server
choices.feedback: The remote group and remote server selectors are mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: What does phRecvTime represent in FortiSIEM?

choices.text: The time the platform first received the event
choices.feedback: FortiSIEM defines phRecvTime as the first-received timestamp used by platform functionality.

choices.text: The source device's original event-generation timestamp
choices.feedback: The source event timestamp is separate from receive time.

choices.text: The time an analyst first opened the incident
choices.feedback: Analyst view time is not the ingestion timestamp.

choices.text: The last time a parser rule was modified
choices.feedback: Parser edit time is unrelated to event lifecycle.

questions.stem: Why must a custom parser leave phRecvTime untouched?

choices.text: Parser may set it only when source time is UTC
choices.feedback: The restriction is about ownership, not UTC formatting.

choices.text: FortiSIEM reserves it as a system-managed event receive-time field
choices.feedback: The 7.5.x documentation explicitly prohibits custom parsers from setting phRecvTime.

choices.text: It is a free-form incident title field for analyst notes
choices.feedback: Incident titles are separate user-facing fields.

choices.text: It is populated from the FortiGate firewall policy identifier
choices.feedback: Firewall policy IDs do not define event receive time.

questions.stem: Which field family should a rule avoid assigning as custom incident attributes?

choices.text: User-defined enrichment fields created for the incident workflow
choices.feedback: User-defined enrichment fields are the intended place for custom values.

choices.text: Custom text fields used for analyst notes and external context
choices.feedback: Custom analyst notes are not the reserved system fields described.

choices.text: System-managed fields such as Incident ID, Status and times
choices.feedback: FortiSIEM reserves lifecycle and system attributes that the platform may overwrite.

choices.text: Business tags that the rule action is allowed to populate
choices.feedback: Permitted business tags can be used for enrichment when configured.

questions.stem: How should an engineer investigate ingestion latency after parsing?

choices.text: Replace phRecvTime with the vendor timestamp in the parser
choices.feedback: Overwriting phRecvTime destroys the system receive-time distinction.

choices.text: Use incident creation time as the only event timestamp
choices.feedback: Incident creation time can occur later and is not the original receive timestamp.

choices.text: Compare parser file modification time with the raw log size
choices.feedback: Parser file time and raw size do not measure event transit delay.

choices.text: Compare source event time with platform phRecvTime for ingestion delay
choices.feedback: Comparing source time with receive time preserves the ingestion-delay signal.

questions.stem: What exact condition triggers the predefined unstable-SPA alert?

choices.text: SLA failure, routing change and BGP-neighbor change all occur
choices.feedback: The FortiSASE handler requires all three telemetry conditions, making it a conjunction.

choices.text: Any single IPsec tunnel-down event occurs at the hub
choices.feedback: A tunnel-down event alone is not the documented trigger.

choices.text: Either an SLA failure or a route change occurs
choices.feedback: The conditions are conjunctive, not OR-based.

choices.text: A user logs in from a different Security PoP
choices.feedback: User location is not one of the three documented signals.

questions.stem: Which prerequisites must exist before testing the SPA alert?

choices.text: Only an email recipient and an enabled dashboard widget
choices.feedback: The dashboard widget is unrelated to SPA service prerequisites.

choices.text: SPA licensing, configured service connection and FortiGate hub
choices.feedback: The guide requires proper SPA licensing/configuration and a FortiGate configured as an SPA hub.

choices.text: A FortiPAM wildcard user and a FortiSIEM incident rule
choices.feedback: Those are unrelated product features.

choices.text: A local FortiGate admin account without an SPA hub
choices.feedback: A local admin account does not provide the SPA hub architecture.

questions.stem: Trigger count increases but no administrator sees an email. What is proven?

choices.text: The BGP neighbor never changed state during the event
choices.feedback: A nonzero trigger count indicates the handler conditions were met.

choices.text: The SPA service connection is still in Configuration State Error
choices.feedback: The service state can recover after the event has fired.

choices.text: The handler fired; email action delivery still needs checking
choices.feedback: Trigger count and Last triggered prove the handler executed, not mailbox delivery.

choices.text: Every Security PoP delivered the email to every recipient
choices.feedback: Email delivery must be verified per configured action and recipient.

questions.stem: A hub tunnel goes down but no unstable-SPA alert fires. What is the best explanation?

choices.text: The handler is designed to alert on any tunnel-down event
choices.feedback: The documented handler is not a single-signal tunnel alarm.

choices.text: FortiSASE ignores all SLA measurements for SPA connections
choices.feedback: SLA failures are explicitly part of the trigger condition.

choices.text: The alert requires an Entra ID group to be synchronized
choices.feedback: Entra group mapping is unrelated to SPA automation.

choices.text: The other required route and BGP signals may be absent
choices.feedback: A tunnel-down event alone does not satisfy the three-condition conjunction.

questions.stem: What makes local-out traffic different from forwarded user traffic?

choices.text: It originates from a FortiGate process, not a LAN session
choices.feedback: Local-out packets originate from FortiGate services such as DNS, NTP and SNMP.

choices.text: It always enters a firewall policy from a client VLAN
choices.feedback: Forwarded user sessions enter from an interface and traverse firewall policy.

choices.text: It uses only the route table and cannot use SD-WAN
choices.feedback: FortiOS supports SD-WAN selection for multiple local-out services.

choices.text: It is generated by remote BGP peers after route convergence
choices.feedback: BGP peers are remote endpoints, not local-out processes.

questions.stem: What does interface-select-method sdwan do for a local service?

choices.text: Pins the service to the first physical WAN interface
choices.feedback: Pinning a physical interface corresponds to specify, not sdwan.

choices.text: Selects egress using SD-WAN or policy-routing rules
choices.feedback: The documented sdwan mode uses SD-WAN or policy-routing rules.

choices.text: Forces the service to use the management interface only
choices.feedback: Management-interface pinning is not the meaning of sdwan mode.

choices.text: Disables policy routing and uses a static route exclusively
choices.feedback: The mode does not disable policy routing.

questions.stem: Why can a source-specific SD-WAN rule miss FortiGate-originated DNS?

choices.text: DNS is always treated as a forwarded TCP session
choices.feedback: DNS local-out is not a forwarded TCP session.

choices.text: SD-WAN rules cannot match locally generated traffic at all
choices.feedback: FortiOS supports local-out services using SD-WAN rules.

choices.text: The DNS source address may be unresolved during rule matching
choices.feedback: Local-out source identity must be selected before a source-based rule can match.

choices.text: The DNS server changes FortiGate source after packet egress
choices.feedback: The source is selected by FortiGate before transmission, not changed by the server.

questions.stem: Which evidence helps inspect local-out policy-route matching?

choices.text: Inspect only the wireless VAP multicast group table
choices.feedback: Wireless multicast state is unrelated to local-out routing.

choices.text: Use only the FortiManager certificate inventory page
choices.feedback: Certificate inventory is unrelated to routing.

choices.text: Check only the FortiAnalyzer deleted-device local event log
choices.feedback: The deletion event log is unrelated to local service egress.

choices.text: Review diagnose firewall proute list and its hit counters
choices.feedback: The route-policy list and counters help prove whether the local-out packet matched a policy route.

questions.stem: Which source hierarchy satisfies the report's evidence rules?

choices.text: Fortinet admin guides for lessons; Community for scenarios
choices.feedback: The lesson feature mechanics come from Fortinet administration/configuration documentation; Community material is scenario-only.

choices.text: Community troubleshooting posts as the primary feature specification
choices.feedback: Community articles are not promoted to primary lesson sources.

choices.text: Search snippets without source links as the sole evidence
choices.feedback: Search snippets are discovery aids, not sufficient source records.

choices.text: Vendor-neutral blogs as the primary configuration authority
choices.feedback: Vendor-neutral sources cannot replace authoritative Fortinet product docs.

questions.stem: What is the strongest completion criterion for a feature-specific test?

choices.text: Confirm the configuration command was accepted by the CLI
choices.feedback: A parser accepting syntax does not prove runtime behavior.

choices.text: Verify the mechanism, its state transition and the resulting evidence
choices.feedback: A good test follows the actual mechanism and confirms the evidence that proves the intended result.

choices.text: Observe one successful ping and infer all related services work
choices.feedback: One ping cannot validate every application, control-plane or auth path.

choices.text: Rely on a green dashboard icon without checking the transaction
choices.feedback: A dashboard status is only one observable and may not prove the transaction.
